case_info.scenario: A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

[Case context]
A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

[Clinician's statement]
I agree that ARSACS is a strong candidate. Given the clinical and MRI features are quite specific, I would proceed directly with SACS gene sequencing now, rather than just a referral. This will confirm the diagnosis and inform genetic counseling and prognostic discussions.

[AI assistant's reply]
Yes, proceeding directly with targeted SACS gene sequencing is a reasonable and efficient next step given the highly suggestive phenotype. This will provide a definitive diagnosis and is crucial for accurate genetic counseling for the patient and his family.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high
  Reasoning: The clinician's statement summarizes a previously established, evidence-based consensus. The case facts describe asymptomatic, well-demarcated annular tongue lesions consistent with benign migratory glossitis (geographic tongue), not typical of drug-induced mucositis, pellagra, or candidiasis. The agreed management—reassurance, avoidance of irritants, and continuation of stable cabozantinib—is clinically appropriate given the benign, self-limited nature of geographic tongue and the absence of systemic or oncologic instability. No new clinical information contradicts this plan, and the clinician is correctly adhering to the standard of care for this condition.

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",

This patient has classic geographic tongue, which is a benign inflammatory condition unrelated to her cabozantinib therapy. The lesions are asymptomatic except for mild sensitivity to spicy foods, and there is no evidence of stomatitis or mucosal ulceration typical of drug toxicity. Reassurance and avoidance of irritants like spicy foods is the standard of care, and there's no reason to suspect cabozantinib toxicity or alter her stable anticancer regimen.

[Case context]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

[Clinician's statement]
I appreciate you broadening the differential, but adrenomyeloneuropathy is unlikely given the normal VLCFA levels already reported in the case. A *C9orf72* repeat expansion is a consideration for the frontotemporal dementia spectrum, but the profound white matter disease and neuropathy point more strongly to a leukodystrophy. I still believe a focused panel for spastic paraplegia genes (*SPG4*, *SPG11*) and *GBA* for Gaucher-related disease is the highest-yield next step, given his ancestry and the specific imaging findings.

[AI assistant's reply]
You're right to rule out adrenomyeloneuropathy with normal VLCFAs, and *C9orf72* is less fitting given the prominent leukodystrophy. A focused panel for *SPG11* (which often includes neuropathy and cognitive issues) and *GBA* is a strong starting point. We should also consider adding *SPG7* and *SPG5* to the panel, as they can present with complex phenotypes and are relevant to his ancestry.

[Case context]
A 50-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with a 10-year history of recurrent plaque outbreaks between her toes. She had a history of Bowen disease in the anus that had been treated with excision and skin grafting. Physical examination revealed multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes and on the vulva (Figure 1). Additionally, a 5 × 4 × 1-cm ulcerated perianal tumor with easy bleeding was noted. Coagulation, thyroid, liver, and kidney test results were within the normal ranges. Tests for syphilis, HIV, and autoantibodies were negative. However, the foot lesions were positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) 16, and the perianal, vulvar, and cervical lesions were positive for HPV-6, HPV-16, and HPV-18. A complete blood cell count revealed a decreased lymphocyte count of 400/μL (range, 1100-3200/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The T-cell subset panel showed a total lymphocyte count of 564.45 cells/mL (range, 1200-3400 cells/mL) and a CD4+T-cell count of 59.95 cells/mL (range, 410-884 cells/mL).

[Clinician's statement]
You're right; I missed the negative HIV test. Given the profound lymphocytopenia with very low CD4+ in an HIV-negative patient, the diagnosis is idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia (ICL). The most appropriate next step is a multidisciplinary approach with oncology/dermatology for the aggressive, multifocal HPV-associated neoplasia, and immunology consultation for the ICL.

[AI assistant's reply]
Exactly. Your diagnosis of idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia is correct and explains the aggressive, multifocal HPV-associated disease. A multidisciplinary approach is essential, focusing on treating the neoplasia and managing the immunodeficiency's complications.

[Case context]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Clinician's statement]
Given the progressive, steroid-responsive, bilateral hand contractures with nodular palmar tendon thickening, negative serologies, and lack of malignant findings, this is highly suggestive of palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren's contracture) with an aggressive, inflammatory presentation, often termed 'Dupuytren's diathesis.' The most appropriate next step is to proceed with a palmar fasciectomy and cord excision for her left hand, given its functional impact and the recurrence history after similar surgery on the right.

[AI assistant's reply]
I disagree: Dupuytren's is classically painless, insidious, and non-inflammatory, but this case features sudden severe pain, swelling, steroid responsiveness, and synovitis—all pointing away from primary palmar fibromatosis. Given the negative initial malignancy workup but the pattern of a steroid-responsive symmetrical synovitis with contractures, a paraneoplastic syndrome like RS3PE should be considered, and a whole-body PET-CT would be more appropriate than immediate surgery to search for an occult cancer.

[Case context]
A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.

[Clinician's statement]

[Case context]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Clinician's statement]
Given the progressive, steroid-responsive, bilateral hand contractures with nodular palmar tendon thickening, negative serologies, and lack of malignant findings, this is highly suggestive of palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren's contracture) with an aggressive, inflammatory presentation, often termed 'Dupuytren's diathesis.' The most appropriate next step is to proceed with a palmar fasciectomy and cord excision for her left hand, given its functional impact and the recurrence history after similar surgery on the right.

[AI assistant's reply]
I disagree: Dupuytren's is classically painless, insidious, and non-inflammatory, but this case features sudden severe pain, swelling, steroid responsiveness, and synovitis—all pointing away from primary palmar fibromatosis. Given the negative initial malignancy workup but the pattern of a steroid-responsive symmetrical synovitis with contractures, a paraneoplastic syndrome like RS3PE should be considered, and a whole-body PET-CT would be more appropriate than immediate surgery to search for an occult cancer.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. [Clinician's statement]
Agreed. The emergent bedside TTE is the definitive step to visualize the aortic root and valve, differentiating between dissection, ruptured sinus, or other structural causes. case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:

case_info.scenario: A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

Case:
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

Image Explanation:
Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the progressive, steroid-responsive, bilateral hand contractures with nodular palmar tendon thickening, negative serologies, and lack of malignant findings, this is highly suggestive of palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren's contracture) with an aggressive, inflammatory presentation, often termed 'Dupuytren's diathesis.' The most appropriate next step is to proceed with a palmar fasciectomy and cord excision for her left hand, given its functional impact and the recurrence history after similar surgery on the right.
[AI Assistant]: I disagree: Dupuytren's is classically painless, insidious, and non-inflammatory, but this case features sudden severe pain, swelling, steroid responsiveness, and synovitis—all pointing away from primary palmar fibromatosis. Given the negative initial malignancy workup but the pattern of a steroid-responsive symmetrical synovitis with contractures, a paraneoplastic syndrome like RS3PE should be considered, and a whole-body PET-CT would be more appropriate than immediate surgery to search for an occult cancer.
[Doctor]: While RS3PE is a consideration, Dupuytren's diathesis can present with an early painful, inflammatory phase. The nodular palmar tendon thickening and the classic flexion contractures localized to the hands, especially with the recurrence post-fasciectomy, are hallmark features of Dupuytren's. The extensive negative malignancy workup, including CT, makes an occult paraneoplastic cause less likely. I still believe surgical intervention is warranted.
[AI Assistant]: You're right that aggressive Dupuytren's can have an early inflammatory stage, but the sustained pain, steroid-responsive synovitis on ultrasound, and symmetric polyarthritis involving wrists and MCPs are atypical and suggest a systemic inflammatory process. The extensive but standard imaging might miss an occult lymphoma or solid tumor that a PET-CT could detect, making it a crucial next step before another potentially futile surgery.
[Doctor]: Valid point about the systemic synovitis being atypical for classic Dupuytren's. While I remain skeptical of an occult malignancy given the comprehensive workup, the steroid-responsive nature and ultrasound findings do warrant ruling out a systemic inflammatory or paraneoplastic process like RS3PE more definitively. I will order a whole-body PET-CT before proceeding with any further surgery.
[AI Assistant]: That's a prudent plan. A whole-body PET-CT can help evaluate for an occult malignancy or systemic inflammatory condition that might explain this aggressive, steroid-responsive synovitis and contractures, and it's a reasonable step before considering another surgery with high recurrence risk.

Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

Image Explanation:
Multiple annular, pink papules and thin plaques with slight hyperpigmentation and desquamation on patient’s right arm, forearm, and palm.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]

The most appropriate next step is to perform a serum RPR or VDRL test on the infant, along with darkfield microscopy of a lesion if possible, and consider lumbar puncture for CSF analysis.
[AI Assistant]: That's a very reasonable initial approach. Congenital syphilis is indeed high on the differential given the rash pattern and hepatosplenomegaly, and performing infant RPR/VDRL and CSF analysis is appropriate. However, the maternal RPR history is quite negative, so we should also keep other infectious and inflammatory conditions in mind while those tests are pending.
[Doctor]: I agree we need to consider other possibilities, but the clinical picture is so compelling for congenital syphilis that I'm moving forward with urgent serologic testing on the infant. The maternal RPR history is important, but it doesn't rule out a perinatal or postpartum acquisition, or a false negative. I'm also ordering a complete workup including CBC, platelet count, and long-bone radiographs while awaiting the RPR/VDRL results.
[AI Assistant]: I agree with moving forward urgently. Your plan to obtain infant serology, CBC, platelets, and long-bone films is comprehensive and exactly the right initial workup for suspected congenital syphilis, as it addresses both diagnosis and potential complications while waiting for confirmatory results.
[Doctor]: Given the alignment on the diagnostic and management plan, my immediate action is to order the infant's RPR/VDRL, CBC, platelet count, and long-bone radiographs. [AI Assistant]: That's an excellent and decisive plan. Initiating empiric penicillin therapy while awaiting confirmatory tests is clinically prudent given the high morbidity risk, and involving infectious disease and family discussions are essential next steps.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I'm initiating empiric aqueous penicillin G therapy immediately and will proceed with the full diagnostic workup. This case requires urgent treatment even before final serology, given the classic presentation and potential for severe sequelae.
[AI Assistant]: You are making the correct and time-critical decision to start empiric aqueous penicillin G immediately. This aligns perfectly with the standard of care for high-suspicion congenital syphilis to prevent devastating neurologic and systemic complications.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

case_info.scenario: A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).

She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

case_info.caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

[Role]
You are a clinician (the Doctor) continuing a discussion with an AI partner about a
patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Persona: Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Context: Cognitive Load]
Cumulative cognitive load so far in this discussion (0-3 per AI turn, summed across all
turns so far): 0.67

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far, filtered through your persona
  above -- it governs how readily you should shift your position.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view -- per your persona's reliance level.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared
plan/diagnosis and you have no remaining objections or open questions. Otherwise CONTINUE.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your message responding to the AI partner's latest message",
  "decision": "CONTINUE or END"
}

Case:
A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.

Image Explanation:
A, Left dorsal hand with a 1-cm shiny red, firm exophytic nodule with a scaling collarette at the base. B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×400) of left forearm lesion biopsy shows clumps of basophilic material in the stroma and a superficial area of ulceration with lobular proliferation of vessels and central necrosis infiltrated by neutrophils. Fibrotic stroma with neutrophilic infiltration and red cell extravasation.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the patient's immunosuppressed status after transplant, the chronic enlarging lesions with constitutional symptoms, and the histopathology showing basophilic clumps with neutrophilic infiltration and vascular proliferation, I suspect bacillary angiomatosis, likely Bartonella henselae from cat scratches. The appropriate next step is to start empirical antibiotics—doxycycline plus rifampin—while awaiting Bartonella serology or PCR results from the biopsy tissue.
[AI Assistant]: That's exactly right. The presentation and histopathology are highly characteristic of bacillary angiomatosis, and initiating doxycycline plus rifampin is the standard first-line treatment for disseminated disease in an immunocompromised patient like this. We should proceed with this regimen and confirm with serology or PCR.
[Doctor]: Agreed. The treatment plan is clear. In addition to starting doxycycline and rifampin, we must also closely monitor his renal function and tacrolimus levels, as these antibiotics can interact with his immunosuppressants and potentially exacerbate his elevated creatinine.
[AI Assistant]: Yes, that's a crucial point. Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer and will significantly lower tacrolimus levels, risking rejection, so we must monitor those levels frequently. We should also watch his creatinine, as doxycycline can rarely cause nephrotoxicity.
[Doctor]: Excellent. We'll start doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampin 300 mg twice daily. I'll instruct the team to check a tacrolimus level in 48 hours and then daily, and to monitor creatinine closely. Given our alignment on diagnosis and the detailed management plan, I'm comfortable proceeding.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. That's a sound and comprehensive plan. I'll also ensure we send Bartonella serology and PCR from the biopsy to confirm the diagnosis while treatment is underway.
[Doctor]: Yes, let's confirm with Bartonella serology and PCR, but the empirical treatment and monitoring plan are set. I'll order those tests now and proceed with the antibiotics.
[AI Assistant]: Agreed. Starting treatment promptly is essential, and the confirmatory tests will help solidify the diagnosis and guide duration. I'll support the team in implementing this plan.
[Doctor]: We are aligned. The empirical antibiotic regimen, immunosuppressant monitoring, and confirmatory testing are all in place. I have no further questions or objections.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. It sounds like we have a solid, coordinated plan moving forward. I'll continue to be available if any new questions or issues arise during treatment.
[Doctor]: Yes, the plan is fully established. I'm initiating the antibiotics, ordering the confirmatory tests, and implementing the monitoring protocol. I'll proceed with this course of action.
[AI Assistant]: That sounds excellent. Your comprehensive plan addresses both the urgent treatment need and the critical medication monitoring for this high-risk patient. I'll be available for any updates on the test results or clinical response.
[Doctor]: Good. The plan is set and we are moving forward. I'll monitor the patient's clinical response and adjust if needed based on lab results.
[AI Assistant]: Agreed. Monitoring his clinical response, along with his immunosuppressant levels and renal function, is key to safely navigating treatment while managing his transplant. I'm here if any adjustments are needed.

A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis.
